result.summary: Diagnosed GH-752/ISS-0692 as a HOST-CAPACITY contention issue that masquerades as a deterministic test-integration failure. ISS-0665's fix (BPM_TEST_STMT_TIMEOUT=300s default) is structurally correct and IS doing what it was designed to do (broaden the DDL window against ~65s statement-timeout cancellations), but on THIS host under full ~40-binary concurrency, that default is still insufficient for the simultaneous lock-acquisition storm. The host exhibits a stark concurrency gradient (52 failures at full → 2 failures at -j4 → 2 failures at -j4-repeat), which is the signature of host-CPU/I/O contention, NOT a deterministic code regression. Chosen mitigation is a COMBINATION of (b) PRIMARY + (a) AUXILIARY: add a default -j cap to the test-integration build step in build.zig (with an env-var escape hatch) so the host does not get asked to schedule ~40 binaries simultaneously; AND raise the BPM_TEST_STMT_TIMEOUT default from 300s to 600s as a secondary safety net for the residual queue depth after the -j cap. Mitigation (c) was investigated but the assembled lock-release path (defer + catch{} on every error branch in runMigrations / runMigrationsForSchema) is already correct; the ungranted locks reported after a CANCELLED run are leftover from process termination (test runner hard-kills the binary), which bypasses defer. Mitigation (c) as a code change is therefore NOT actionable; the ungranted-lock leak is a CONSEQUENCE of the cancellation storm that mitigation (b) prevents, not an independent defect.

evidence_chain.detail: ISS-0665 mitigation holder reported 52 failures at full concurrency → 2 failures at -j4 → 2 failures at -j4-repeat, on the SAME commit, byte-identical code. This is a textbook capacity-contention pattern: failures drop ~26x when scheduling concurrency is reduced ~10x. A deterministic code regression would NOT show this gradient.

Failures cluster as PgError.ServerError during pg_advisory_lock(hashtext('bpm_test_migrations_public')) acquisition in tests/integration/helpers.zig. The advisory lock is the shared bottleneck — every binary queues behind it for the duration of the migration DDL. The 'test runner failed to respond for ~1m<N>ms' entries are Zig's build runner killing stragglers that exceed its own per-step timeout, NOT a test logic failure.
evidence_chain.source: tests/integration/helpers.zig lines 121-165 (runMigrations advisory lock + statement_timeout bracket)

evidence_chain.evidence: 60s ambient timeout still bites non-DDL work
evidence_chain.detail: ISS-0665 broadened the DDL window only (SET statement_timeout = BPM_TEST_STMT_TIMEOUT bracketed around the migration calls). Every OTHER query that the harness runs during init keeps the configureSessionTimeouts() ambient of 60s. Under heavy contention, ANY of those queries — e.g. the public.tenant_schemas / public.schema_migrations COUNT probes that gate the runForSchema fast path (lines ~243-275) — can exceed 60s and be cancelled. The 300s DDL window therefore does not protect the full TestHarness.init() critical section.
evidence_chain.source: tests/integration/helpers.zig lines 210-225 (runMigrationsForSchema timeout bracket) + line 304 (configureSessionTimeouts default 60s) + lines 243-275 (fast-path probes)

evidence_chain.detail: ISS-0665.json names-and-shames the same symptom tree (ISS-0107, ISS-0110, ISS-0151, ISS-0659) and lands the right code shape: bracket a wider timeout around EXACTLY the contended operation, restore the ambient immediately after. The 300s default was a reasonable server-class starting point; on this host's full concurrency, the contention window is larger than 300s on the slowest binary.

evidence_chain.evidence: lock-release path is correct (mitigation c investigation)
evidence_chain.detail: runMigrations() and runMigrationsForSchema() both release the advisory lock via `defer conn.exec("SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(...)", ...) catch {};` placed AFTER the SET statement_timeout bracket. The `defer` runs on every ZIG error path; the `catch {}` swallows any DB error during unlock so the unlock attempt itself cannot escalate the failure. The release path is therefore complete. The ungranted locks after a CANCELLED run are leftover from PROCESS termination (Zig test runner hard-kills the binary after its per-step timeout fires), which bypasses Zig's defer. Mitigation (c) as a code change is not actionable without rewriting the test-runner termination semantics.

evidence_chain.evidence: build.zig test-integration step has no -j default
evidence_chain.detail: build.zig line 2371 declares `test_integration_step = b.step("test-integration", ...)` and aggregates ~40 binaries via dependOn. Zig's build runner defaults to N-1 jobs on N CPU cores; on this host that means ~40 binaries are scheduled simultaneously. There is no project-level -j cap; the only knob is the operator remembering to pass -j4 on every invocation. This is a host-dependent reliability hazard that the build file itself should not expose.

diagnosis.failure_category: E — environment / host capacity contention (not a code regression; not a test logic defect; not a missing requirement)

chosen_mitigation.primary: (b) add a default -j cap to the test-integration build step in build.zig with an env-var escape hatch (BPM_TEST_INTEGRATION_JOB_CAP, default 8); honor `b.option(u32, "test-integration-jobs", ...)` for the deterministic CI setting
chosen_mitigation.secondary: (a) raise BPM_TEST_STMT_TIMEOUT default from 300s to 600s in tests/integration/helpers.zig lines ~139 and ~217, keeping the env-var override intact
chosen_mitigation.rejected: (c) no code change — defer/catch unlock path is already correct; leftover ungranted locks are a CONSEQUENCE of the cancellation storm that mitigation (b) prevents, not an independent defect
chosen_mitigation.rationale: The concurrency gradient is the strongest single evidence this is a host-capacity issue. Reducing concurrency (b) addresses the root cause; raising the per-DDL timeout (a) is a secondary safety net for any residual queue depth after the -j cap. Adopting only (a) would still schedule ~40 binaries competing for the same DB; the contention window would merely be 2x larger — the storm would still blow through it on a fully-loaded host. Adopting only (b) without (a) leaves the residual queue depth at the new -j-bound, which is still enough to time out a 300s DDL window on the slowest binary of a worst-case batch. Adopting (c) is not a code change — the unlock path is already correct; the leak is symptom, not cause.
